title: A Day at the Championships
tagline: Ten events, one hall and a silence you can hear. What memory sport asks of people, and which tool you would pick for each event.
card: The ten standard events of memory championships, and a tool from this course for every one.
goal: you will learn the ten standard events, match each to the tool it needs, and plan a small personal test event of your own.

left_off.q: What are the five steps for a book or article?
left_off.a: Survey, map, place, read and add, test.

left_off.q: What should a palace hold from a book?
left_off.a: The key ideas, not every detail.

left_off.q: Why do you use your own words in a summary?
left_off.a: It forces you to understand, which makes the memory last.

text: London, 1991. A small group of people sit at tables in a hall and wait for a signal. Nobody has done this before. There is no rule book yet worth the name. A writer on mind and learning, Tony Buzan, and a chess master and organiser, Raymond Keene, have invited a few people who claim to have unusual memories to compete in the first World Memory Championship.

The winner is a young Englishman who has trained in secret, using the methods of Roman orators and a system of his own: Dominic O'Brien, whom you met in room 8. He will win it eight times. But what is important is not who wins. It is that the old art has become a sport, with scores and a clock.

check.a: The first World Memory Championship was held, and Dominic O'Brien won it.

parts.talk: Do you think memory should be a sport? What do you think it measures?

text: Since then the championship has grown into an international event, with national contests and young competitors from many countries. The events have settled into a standard programme of ten. Some use words, some use digits, some use cards, faces or images, and a few last an hour while others last seconds.

What strikes a visitor is the quiet. Competitors wear ear defenders, or headphones, to block noise. They sit still. When the clock starts, they are not memorising in the old sense of repeating. They are building and placing pictures, at the speed of a person turning pages.

check.q: What is the atmosphere of a championship like?
check.a: Very quiet: competitors wear ear defenders and sit still, building and placing pictures.

parts.talk: Would you like to watch a memory championship? To compete in one?

text: You do not need to compete to learn from them. The ten events are a catalogue of kinds of memory, and each is a practical question. How do you keep a list of words? A sequence of faces? A run of binary digits? A set of dates? Each event was designed to be hard, and each has a method.
In this room you will go through all ten, match each to the tool from this course, and set up a small event of your own as a personal test.

check.q: Why are the ten events useful to learners?
check.a: They are a catalogue of kinds of memory task, and each has a method you can learn.

parts.talk: Which of the ten kinds of task would be most useful in your daily life?

method.x: The exact rules change from year to year, so check the current rules if you want to compete. The point for us is the training idea: every event is a skill that is trained, not a gift.

method.title: A personal test event
method.given: A ten-minute test you can run at home once a week.
lines: Twenty words, five minutes to study, five to recall.
Six faces and names from a magazine.
Ten cards from a shuffled pack.
Count what you recalled. Write the numbers in a log. Aim to improve each week by one or two items.
method.pic: A small weekly test shows progress that daily practice does not show.

try.title: Design a personal test
try.prompt: Write a ten-minute weekly test using at least three of the ten events. State what you will study, how long, and how you will score it.
try.model: Weekly test: 20 random words (5 min study, 3 min recall); 5 faces and names (3 min); 10 cards in order (3 min). Score: one point per correct item; record total.
checks: At least three events are used.
There is a score and a log.

try.title: Binary digits in threes
try.prompt: The binary row 1 1 0 1 0 0 1 1 1 has nine digits. Group it into three groups of three, and give each group a picture (for example 110, 100, 111). Write your pictures.
try.model: Groups: 110, 100, 111. Pictures: 110 = a tin (one-one-oh); 100 = a hundred-pound note; 111 = three candles. Three pictures for nine digits.
checks: I can read the pictures back as digits.
